segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: These sequences come from three films of the mid-1950s: Pickup on South Street (1953), Kiss Me Deadly (1955) and Invasion of the Body Snatchers (1956), shown in American theaters during the country's most troubled era, capturing the psychological atmosphere of a nation in the age of the Cold War and McCarthyism. The arrival of the House Un-American Activities Committee (HUAC) in Hollywood in September 1947 left the studio heads trembling with fear. At a secret meeting at the Waldorf Astoria hotel in New York in November of that year, they adopted a policy of cooperation.

The arrival of the House Un-American Activities Committee (HUAC) in Hollywood in September nineteen forty-seven left the studio heads trembling with fear. segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: Often cited as the first Cold War film, The Iron Curtain (1948), directed by William Wellman (1896-1975), is a relatively sober story based on the real events of a spy ring in Canada. The political brutality present in many of the films that followed is reflected in titles such as The Red Menace (1949), directed by R.G. Springsteen (1904-1989), in which a war veteran is lured in by communist spies, or I Was a Communist for the FBI (1951), by Gordon Douglas (1907-1993), about an undercover agent infiltrating the Communist Party. With cheap budgets and no big stars, the studios' propaganda pieces seemed almost like an excuse.

segments.original: The Woman on Pier 13 (1949), whose original title was I Married a Communist until the studio decided to change it, directed by Robert Stevenson (1905-1986), was offered by Howard Hughes to several directors as a loyalty test. The absurdities of the screenplay are offset by Nicholas Musuraca's (1892-1975) noir-style cinematography and by the cast headed by Robert Ryan (1909-1973).

segments.original: In the summer of 1947, newspapers reported that unidentified wreckage had been found in New Mexico, giving rise to the first wave of UFO paranoia. Alien invasion plots in science fiction films reflected Cold War anxieties. The Thing from Another World (1951), directed by Christian Nyby (1913-1993) but credited to producer Howard Hawks, shows blood-drinking aliens unwittingly brought to a research station in the Arctic. Its final line, "Watch the skies, everywhere!", could be read as a warning to the nation.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: It Came from Outer Space (1953) is more ambiguous: the aliens are relatively benign, but they temporarily inhabit human bodies. Invasion of the Body Snatchers (1956), with its hordes of aliens imitating their human hosts, can be seen as a metaphor for the communist threat or for the frightening American conformity under McCarthyism.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: Jack Arnold's (1916-1992) The Incredible Shrinking Man (1957) is the most touching metaphor for mid-20th-century America's jitters. A Los Angeles businessman notices that he is beginning to shrink - an irreversible consequence of nuclear contamination. On his journey toward disappearance, he ends up living in a dollhouse that mimics his own suburban home and faces his final struggle for survival in the basement, a speck amid the debris of American life.

segments.speaker: narrador
segments.original: In the 1960s, it seemed possible that some of the political ghosts might be exorcised. John Frankenheimer's (1930-2002) The Manchurian Candidate (1962) portrayed a McCarthy-like senator as a buffoon used to bring about the communist domination of the United States, and Emile de Antonio's (1920-1989) Point of Order (1964) used television footage of the Army-McCarthy hearings to reveal the truth about McCarthyism. By then, the Cuban Missile Crisis and the Kennedy assassination meant that the fears of the 1950s had taken another form.
